Grand jury indicts Mexican national for firearm possession after Dallas ISD officer shooting
A Mexican national has been indicted by a federal grand jury after allegedly shooting a Dallas ISD police officer during an attempted escape last month. Authorities say Jose Santiago Pantoja-Morales faces up to 15 years if convicted on firearms charges related to being an illegal alien found with a weapon.
A federal grand jury indicted Jose Santiago Pantoja-Morales, a 27-year-old Mexican national, for possession of a firearm by an illegal alien after he allegedly shot a Dallas Independent School District police officer while attempting to flee, according to an announcement by United States Attorney for the Northern District of Texas Ryan Raybould on Sep. 23.
Raybould said, “The illegal alien’s alleged actions in this case represent an attack on the rule of law and a direct threat to public safety. Every day, we ask the men and women who wear the badge to stand between good and evil. It is my duty—and the duty of this office—to do all we can to protect those who protect us. Violence against an officer will not be tolerated, and we will pursue this prosecution with the utmost rigor to ensure full accountability.”
According to authorities, on Aug. 6 Pantoja-Morales allegedly jumped out of his co-worker’s vehicle into the center median of Lyndon B. Johnson Freeway. His co-worker flagged down a Dallas ISD officer who was on routine patrol; that officer gave Pantoja-Morales a ride to a nearby safe location. During transport, Pantoja-Morales allegedly began rummaging through the officer’s bag in the back seat. The officer stopped and attempted to remove him from the vehicle but was met with resistance, leading to a physical struggle.
During this altercation, as described in court documents filed Aug. 13, Pantoja-Morales allegedly grabbed the officer’s firearm and fired one shot at him, striking his femoral artery in his right leg. The injured officer regained control of his weapon while Pantoja-Morales fled but was quickly apprehended by law enforcement officers nearby. A fellow Dallas ISD officer provided medical treatment before emergency services transported him for further care at Parkland Hospital.
ATF Dallas Field Division Special Agent in Charge Brian Garner said, “An officer who was simply doing his job was violently attacked and shot. This case underscores the danger law enforcement officers face every day and the consequences when a firearm is placed in the hands of someone who is prohibited from possessing one. ATF will continue working alongside our law enforcement partners to investigate these cases and ensure those who violate federal firearms laws are held accountable.”
The grand jury returned its indictment on Sept. 16; Pantoja-Morales remains pending transfer to federal custody pursuant to a writ of habeas corpus filed that day. If convicted, he faces up to 15 years in federal prison.
The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives-Dallas Field Office and Dallas Police Department conducted this investigation while Assistant U.S. Attorney Nadin-Sarah Salkic prosecutes it.
An indictment is merely an allegation; defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty in court.
The U.S Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Texas covers approximately 96,000 square miles serving about eight million residents across northern Texas with facilities located at Earle Cabell Federal Building in Dallas as well as branch offices in Fort Worth, Lubbock, Amarillo and Abilene; it employs around 100 assistant attorneys along with support staff tasked with prosecuting federal crimes and managing civil litigation for government interests as part of its role within the U.S Department of Justice while also promoting community trust through outreach initiatives, according to its official website.
